title: US Inflation Just Hit 3.8 Per Cent. Markets Are Now Pricing a Fed Rate Hike Over a Cut. Here Is What That Means for NRI Investors.
excerpt: The April PCE reading is the highest since May 2023. The S&P 500 has risen for nine straight weeks anyway. On June 5, both the US jobs report and the RBI rate decision land on the same day. Your portfolio in both countries is on the line.
body:
The number that landed on Thursday changed the conversation. The Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index — the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge — rose 3.8 per cent in the 12 months through April 2026. That is the highest reading since May 2023, and it is nearly double the Fed's 2 per cent target.

The cause is not a mystery. The US-Iran conflict, now in its fourth month, has kept Brent crude hovering near $91 a barrel. The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20 per cent of the world's oil supply passes, remains effectively closed. Energy prices are bleeding into everything — transport costs, food prices, manufacturing inputs, and the heating and cooling bills that American households pay every month.

For NRI investors holding assets in both countries, the coming week is unusually consequential. On June 5, two decisions land on the same day: the US non-farm payrolls report and the Reserve Bank of India's monetary policy announcement. Together, they will shape interest rates, currency values, and equity markets on both sides of the world.

## The Fed's Dilemma

Markets have shifted dramatically. Investors now see a greater chance of a Federal Reserve rate hike than a rate cut in 2026, according to LSEG data, which shows a 59 per cent probability of a rate increase by year-end. This is a reversal from the start of the year, when rate cuts were the consensus expectation.

Kevin Warsh, who took over as Fed chair earlier in 2026, faces his first meeting later in June. His reputation as a hawk — he has historically favoured tighter monetary policy — adds to the expectation that the Fed will lean towards restraint rather than stimulus.

The May jobs report, expected on June 5, will be critical. Economists polled by Reuters expect 85,000 to 96,000 new jobs and an unemployment rate of 4.3 per cent. A stronger number could cement rate hike expectations. A weaker one could revive recession fears.

"If you were to get a hot employment report alongside still-rising inflation numbers, I think it continues to change the outlook for Fed policy," said Liz Ann Sonders, chief investment strategist at the Schwab Center for Financial Research. "If it were to be a weaker-than-expected report, then maybe it calms fears that the Fed is going to have to shift to a tightening stance."

## The Stock Market Does Not Seem to Care

Despite the inflation data, US equities have been on a tear. The S&P 500 has posted gains for nine consecutive weeks and is up more than 10 per cent for the year. The Nasdaq Composite has climbed 16 per cent, driven by an AI-powered rally in technology stocks.

Broadcom reports earnings next week, and its results will test whether the AI trade — which has been the single largest driver of the US stock market in 2026 — can sustain its momentum. Technology stocks corrected sharply in March but have roared back as investors concluded that earnings growth remained intact.

The disconnect between surging stocks and rising inflation is not new, but it is becoming harder to ignore. Higher bond yields, driven by inflation expectations, are the mechanism through which this tension eventually resolves. The 10-year Treasury yield has climbed to 4.51 per cent, and any further rise would increase borrowing costs across the economy and put pressure on stock valuations.

## What This Means for India

India is caught in the crossfire. As the world's third-largest oil importer, the Hormuz disruption has hit the economy hard. The rupee is down roughly 6 per cent for the year. Foreign investors have pulled more than $24 billion from Indian debt and equities between March and May.

On Friday, the rupee rallied to 95 per dollar — its best single-day gain in nearly two months — after the RBI intervened and oil prices dropped on reports of a possible ceasefire extension. But the relief may be temporary.

India's own finance ministry released its monthly economic report on Saturday, warning that retail inflation could accelerate due to recent fuel price hikes and a weaker-than-expected monsoon forecast. The ministry called the duration of the Strait of Hormuz disruption "the single most consequential variable" for India's external and price outlook.

The RBI is expected to hold its key rate at 5.25 per cent on June 5, but a growing minority of economists — 12 out of 56 in a Reuters poll — now expect a rate hike. Capital Economics has pencilled in a repo rate of 6.00 per cent before the end of 2026, contingent on the crisis continuing and energy prices staying elevated.

## What NRI Investors Should Watch

**If both the US jobs report and RBI surprise hawkish on June 5:** Expect the dollar to strengthen, the rupee to weaken further, Indian IT stocks to face selling pressure as US rate hike fears hit their biggest clients, and NRI fixed deposits in India to eventually offer better rates as the RBI tightens.

**If the US jobs report is weak and the RBI holds:** Markets may rally on both sides as rate hike fears recede, but the relief could be short-lived if oil prices remain elevated.

**If the Hormuz truce is extended:** This is the wildcard. A 60-day extension that allows shipping to resume would cause oil prices to drop sharply, ease inflation on both sides, and potentially trigger a rally in Indian equities that Barron's has described as "in the midst of their worst year in three decades in terms of performance versus Asian peers."

The convergence of these events on a single day is rare. NRI investors with exposure to US equities, Indian stocks, NRI deposits, or remittance flows should understand that June 5 is not just another data day. It is the day that the direction of interest rates in both countries could become clear — and with it, the trajectory of every dollar moving between them.
author: Diaspora Desk
